<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
This comment does valuable forensic work on the Halden pilot, and most of its specific corrections hold up. Its final conclusion does not. It moves from "the reported gain is roughly halved in a non-random subset" to "per-hour gains are entirely an artifact," and the evidence it cites, including the Varden trial it praises, doesn't support that step.

## The numbers mostly check out, with two exceptions

**These are correct:**
- Table 2 reproduces exactly: 95.1/0.8 is +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 is +14.6%, and 95.4/0.861 is +10.8%.
- The hours falls are right: 34.6/40.3 is −14.1%, and 34.8/40.4 is −13.9%.
- The real revenue figure is right: 1.014/1.041 = 0.974, a fall of 2.6%.
- "Roughly four points" (3.8) and "roughly six points" (20 vs 14.1) are accurate summaries.

**The hours breakdown doesn't add up.**
- If a scheduled day is 8 hours, four days at +0.7 hours gives 34.8, and adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours. The reported total is 34.6.
- Put another way, the two sources add about 4.4 hours above the 32-hour schedule. The total shows only about 2.6.
- Either the components or the total is wrong, or the components cover different groups of organisations. The headline −14.1% may still be right, but this needs explaining.

**The novelty extrapolation is slightly off.**
- Energy falls from 0.61 SD at month three to 0.29 at month six, about 0.107 SD a month.
- At that rate it reaches zero around month 8.7, not "around month ten".
- This is minor, but it is a two-point straight-line projection presented with more precision than it can carry.

## What it does well

- **Attrition.** The microdata show that seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule started, mostly citing workload. That directly contradicts the working paper's "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". This is the comment's most important finding, and it reflects badly on the original paper.
- **Manager ratings vs records.** In 19 of 23 organisations, the manager's index was higher than the records showed. That is a systematic gap, and the comment handles it fairly without alleging bad faith.
- **Actual hours.** This is the right correction. It also lines up with Varden: hours fell 14.1% here versus 13% in Varden's case-processing offices, with similar sources (longer remaining days, work on the day off).
- **Revenue.** Adjusting for inflation is right. I flagged the same issue in my first review.
- **Sector claims.** It confirms that the per-hour metric produces the "every sector gained" result. I flagged this too.
- **Data note.** It honestly says the corrected figures describe non-random subsets.

## Problems

**1. The abstract claims a correction the table doesn't make.**
The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output and hours) brings the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified, not even as a bound. One option would be to bring back the nine withdrawals at plausible output levels using their early-month data. As written, the 10.8% does not account for attrition at all.

**2. The conclusion goes beyond the evidence.**
After all corrections, a gain of about 11% *remains*. The case for reducing it to zero rests entirely on the novelty argument, and that argument is weak:
- **Energy is not output.** The decline is in self-reported energy, not in productivity. Energy at month six was still 0.29 SD above baseline.
- **The direct test wasn't run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. With the microdata in hand, the authors could have checked whether output per hour fell over the six months. They didn't, and relied on a two-point extrapolation of a different variable.
- **The burden of proof is applied one way.** The comment rightly says six months can't prove a durable effect. By the same logic, it can't prove a zero effect. "Not shown to be durable" is not the same as "entirely an artifact".

**3. It uses the Varden trial selectively.**
- It calls Varden's counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature". The same trial, using the same methods, found a **+12.5% gain per actual hour in case-processing offices (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**.
- That result comes from record-based output, actual hours, a randomised control and nine months of follow-up. It addresses the comment's points about measurement, selection, attrition and duration.
- That figure is close to Halden's corrected 10.8%. Two independent sources point to a real gain of roughly 10–12% in non-coverage work, which is the opposite of "entirely an artifact".
- Varden's staff also didn't choose the change; offices were randomised. That makes it a weaker setting for the "chosen and welcomed" novelty story.
- The comment never mentions this result.

**4. It misrepresents the Varden meetings analysis.**
- **Timing.** The meetings data were collected in month six, at managers' request, *during* the trial. "Selected for analysis after the results were known" isn't accurate. The analysis was unregistered, which is a fair criticism, but that is a different problem.
- **Varden's actual claims.** Varden's authors didn't present meetings as an established mechanism. They said seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.
- **Rebutting a weaker claim.** Warning that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" responds to something Varden didn't say.
- **An internal tension.** The meetings explanation actually fits the comment's sceptical aims. It implies the gain comes from removing wasted time, not from rest, which my earlier calculation suggested could explain much of the per-hour gain. That is a real but different effect, not an artifact. If the comment believes the gains are entirely artificial, there is nothing left for a mechanism to explain. Its strong dismissal suggests it wants the gain to be both artifactual and unexplained.

**5. Record-based output isn't automatically the true figure.**
- One listed record is "billable hours delivered". For a firm cutting hours, that measure falls almost by construction and tracks hours rather than output.
- Counts of tickets or cases ignore complexity and quality.
- The 19-of-23 pattern still suggests manager optimism. But part of the 3.8-point gap may come from limits of the records, not just manager bias.

**6. No uncertainty is reported.**
The comment criticises others' methods but gives no confidence intervals or tests:
- none for the 3.8-point gap,
- none for the 10.8% estimate,
- none for the −11.2% retail figure, which rests on **three organisations**.

The retail figure matching Varden's −11.4% is suggestive, but with n = 3 it could easily be coincidence.

**7. The conclusion reaches beyond the data.**
- The data note correctly says the estimates describe only the subsets analysed.
- The conclusion then generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes", meaning all such schemes. One re-analysed pilot can't support that.
- It also leaves out the sick-day and retention results. These may be selected too, but they matter to whether a scheme is worth having even if output per employee falls slightly.

## Where the three documents leave things

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% per-hour gain | Overstated. Roughly halved by using records and actual hours, and attrition likely reduces it further. |
| Scheduled hours overstate the gain | Confirmed independently by Varden (22% vs 12.5%) and the comment (20% vs 14.1% cut in hours). |
| Reduced hours suit all sectors | Not supported. Coverage-bound work loses about 11% of output per employee (Varden, randomised), consistent with Halden's retail figures. |
| A real per-hour gain in backlog or knowledge work | Supported at roughly 10–12% by Varden's randomised result and Halden's corrected subset. Durability is unknown. |
| The gain is "entirely an artifact" | Not supported. It rests on an untested novelty argument and leaves out Varden's case-processing result. |
| Mechanism: rest vs removing wasted time | Open. The meetings data are suggestive but exploratory, and Varden's 24-month confirmatory test is the right next step. |

Overall, the comment is a useful correction to the Halden paper. Its strongest contribution is showing that the attrition was misreported. Its recommendations for future evaluations are sound and largely describe what Varden already did. Its headline conclusion should be read as an opinion, as the repeated "in our assessment" suggests, not as a finding.
